chapter_theme: தவம் is defined simply as bearing pain and harming no one, and is then credited with immense powers, over enemies, wishes, and even death. The chapter makes it the one truly self-regarding work and the reason so few prosper.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the definition of தவம் (261), its excellence (262-265), the height of those who practise it (266-269), and the lowness of those who don't (270).

261.reading: Bearing the pain that comes and causing no pain to living beings: such alone is the form of தவம்.
261.nuance: The definition mentions no gods, rites or forest, and half of it is ethical. Parimelazhagar takes the pain as self-imposed through such things as reduced food, while Manakkudavar says only pain that has come to one. Kalaignar turns it into a heart that can bear anything, which would make tapas available in any life.

262.reading: தவம் too comes to those who have தவம்; for those without it, taking it up is futile.
262.nuance: The form is circular, a discouraging one for a would-be beginner. The chapter's praise of effort in the following verses sits awkwardly with it.

positions.position: One needs தவம் from an earlier birth, which gives the familiarity needed to complete it.
It requires earlier good deeds of any kind, not earlier austerity as such.
It requires present firmness and self-control, with no former birth involved.

263.reading: Is it in wanting to provide for those who have renounced that the others have forgotten தவம்?
263.nuance: The chiding question implies that தவம் isn't reserved for renunciants. Both older commentators draw the conclusion that தவம் is greater than giving, but the verse only implies it.

positions.position: Householders, drawn by love of giving, have forgotten what is greater.

264.reading: Crushing foes and raising those who rejoice with one come through தவம், if one so intends.
264.nuance: எண்ணின், 'if one thinks of it', is doing much here. Parimelazhagar takes it to imply that such people naturally don't think of it. An ascetic with enemies is a problem for him, and he solves it by moving the power to தவம் itself.

positions.position: The foes are enemies of virtue, and the friends are those who delight in it.
These are ordinary enemies and friends, and the power comes from austerity done earlier.
positions.quote: பகைவரைத் தெறுதலும், நட்டோரையாக்குதலு மாகிய வலி ஆராயின், முன்செய்த தவத்தினாலே வரும்

265.reading: Because whatever is wanted is obtained as it is wanted, தவம் is striven for here.
265.nuance: The motive offered is getting what you want, in a chapter that condemns desire in the very next verse. Parimelazhagar infers from ஈண்டு, 'here', that the results come in the next life and include release, but the verse doesn't say so.

266.reading: Those who do தவம் are doing their own work; the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile.
266.nuance: தங்கருமம் is telling: austerity is presented as true self-interest, and worldly activity as neglect of one's real business. Parimelazhagar adds 'having renounced' and identifies 'the rest' as those pursuing wealth and pleasure, which sweeps in most of life.

267.reading: For those able to endure, pain burning them makes them shine, as gold shines the more it is burned.
267.nuance: The doubled சுடச்சுட appears in both lines and makes the image of repeated firing audible. What the shining stands for is left open: for Parimelazhagar sin leaves and knowledge grows, for Manakkudavar deeds leave, and for Kalaignar it is fame.

268.reading: All other living beings worship the one who has completely gained his own self.
268.nuance: The disagreement is nearly a reversal: for one reading the person comes to own the self, and for the other he is rid of it.

positions.position: He has obtained his own self as truly his own, and அற intensifies this: nothing is harder to obtain.
positions.quote: தன் உயிரைத் தான் தனக்கு உரித்தாகப் பெற்றவனை

positions.position: அற marks cessation: he has got rid of the thought of 'I', and தான் is the ego.
He has neither attachment to 'my life' nor the pride of 'I'.

269.reading: Even leaping past death becomes possible for those who have attained the power of austerity.
269.nuance: Parimelazhagar notes the 'even' can signal how nearly impossible it is. Manakkudavar illustrates with Markandeya, which is his example and isn't in the verse. Kalaignar takes it as conquering death through steadfastness.

270.reading: The reason the have-nots are many: those who practise austerity are few and those who don't are many.
270.nuance: The verse says just 'those who lack', without saying what they lack. As an explanation of poverty it is arresting and severe, and the commentators each soften or redirect it.

positions.position: Wealth and poverty here include having and lacking understanding.
positions.quote: செல்வம் நல்குரவு என்பன ஈண்டு அறிவினது உண்மை இன்மைகளையும் குறித்து நின்றன;

positions.position: It is about those without goods, plainly.
positions.quote: பொருளில்லாதார் உலகத்துப் பலராதற்குக் காரணம், தவஞ் செய்வார் சிலராதல்;

positions.position: It is about those lacking capability, and the few are simply those with firm resolve.

links.note: 225 puts the strength of enduring hunger behind that of removing it, which favours the giver. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar draw from 263 that தவம் exceeds giving. Whatever the verses themselves imply, the commentary tradition faces a real conflict here.

203 calls refraining from harm even to enemies the height of understanding, and 261 defines austerity by harmlessness. Yet 264 advertises the power to crush foes. Parimelazhagar's 'enemies of virtue' and his comment that ascetics don't think of it are attempts to close this gap.

46 asks what a virtuous householder could gain by leaving for the other path. 266 says that those not doing தவம் are doing futile things. The chapters on householding and austerity each claim the highest place.
265 recommends austerity because it gets whatever one wants. 370 says the unchanging state comes from removing desire. The means is sold by appeal to the very thing the end abolishes.
On Manakkudavar's reading of 268, its subject has lost the ego, which is exactly the cutting of 'I' and 'mine' in 346. Parimelazhagar's 'possessing oneself' would make the link weaker.

Two different conquests of death: by the power of austerity in 269, and by the vow of not killing in 326, where death's advance doesn't reach. The Kural offers an ethical route alongside the ascetic one.
270 explains poverty as too little austerity, which is something people could change. 377 says enjoyment is only as the apportioner apportioned. The same fact gets a moral cause and a fatal one.

source_issues: 262: the verse text reads ஆகும் அதனை, while Parimelazhagar's gloss shows அவம் அதனை. The word அவம், on which the sense 'futile' depends, has dropped from the text.
269: the verse text ends டவர்க்குல், an evident misprint for டவர்க்கு.
